title: Lamps burning (Luke 12:35–59)
hookLine: be like servants waiting up for their master

lines: THE MASTER IS AT A WEDDING.
NOBODY KNOWS WHEN HE'LL BE BACK.
cards: A big house, late at night. The master has gone to a wedding feast, and in that world a wedding could run for days, so nobody knows when he'll be back. Midnight?
Three in the morning? The servants could all go to bed. Or they could do what Jesus describes: keep their robes tucked into their belts, the oil lamps trimmed and burning, and listen for a knock.
Anyone who has waited up for a teenager, or sat by the phone for news from a hospital, knows this kind of night.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning." People wore long robes, and to run or work you tucked the hem up into your belt. It's the ancient way of saying roll up your sleeves.

Then the most surprising sentence in the passage: "Blessed are those servants, whom the lord when he cometh shall find watching: verily I say unto you, that he shall gird himself, and make them to sit down to meat, and will come forth and serve them."
The master comes home at midnight, finds his servants awake, and instead of being served, he ties on an apron and serves them dinner. Everything upside down.
Christians hear in it the same Jesus who, in John's Gospel, washes his friends' feet. What are they waiting for?
Most Christians read this as the return of Christ at the end of time, which, Jesus says, comes at an hour when you think not.

teach.h: THE RETURN, AND EVERY ORDINARY DAY.
teach.b: Many also hear it about every ordinary day: being awake to God, and to people, right now. The chapter grows more urgent. "For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required."
You can read the sky and know rain is coming, Jesus says, so why can't you read this moment? And if you have a quarrel, settle it on the way, before it reaches the judge. All of it says one thing.
The knock could come in the middle of any conversation.

how: Christians read watching passages like this one especially in Advent, the season of waiting before Christmas, and many churches keep a candle burning or light a new one each week as a sign of readiness.

o: a sign that the world will soon burn up
lamps left lit to keep thieves away at night
awake and ready, like servants waiting up

games.q: what's inside Luke 12:35–59 — tap the pairs.
p: robe tucked up, ready to move

s: in the story, the master makes the tired servants serve him dinner
he girds himself, sits them down, and comes and serves them.
girded loins means a long robe tucked into the belt, ready for work
the old way of saying roll up your sleeves.
Jesus gives the hour of his return
he says it comes at an hour when you think not.

games.q: you're a master home from a wedding after midnight. your servants are awake, lamps burning. what do you do?
o: tie on an apron and serve them dinner.
games.why: "he shall gird himself, and make them to sit down to meat, and will come forth and serve them." everything upside down.

practice: Be like a servant listening for a knock: notice every sound, a car, a clock, your own breath, and when your mind drifts, bring it back the way you'd jolt upright at footsteps by the door.
Then think of one conversation you usually half listen to, and picture yourself fully awake in it, phone down, eyes up, really hearing. If you pray, ask to be found watching.

wordCard.voice: Lamps burning. Servants waiting up with their robes tucked in and their lights lit, and a master who comes home and serves them.

orig.note: Greek: watching, staying awake. the name Gregory comes from this word family.

carryVoice: Your line: keep your lamps lit. In this story, the master comes home and serves. Day five hundred fifty, done.
